strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing concrete challenges in multi-agent RL for LLMs (credit assignment and advantage estimation variance)
Methodologically sound technical contributions with turn-level advantage estimator and agent-specific normalization cleanly integrated into GRPO
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple levels (games, single-agent benchmarks, multi-agent systems) with proper train/test splits and ablations
Strong empirical results: up to 28.7% improvement on held-out games and meaningful transfer to downstream tasks (10% AIME, 12.5% GPQA-Diamond)
Addresses both cooperative and competitive games, providing better coverage than prior work (SPIRAL) which focused only on zero-sum games
Qualitative analysis demonstrating emergent cognitive skills (role awareness, intent recognition) that transfer across domains
Commitment to reproducibility with code release, detailed implementation details, and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the 'sum-then-normalize' approach is essentially GAE(γ=1, λ=1), and agent-specific normalization is straightforward partitioning by role
Narrow experimental scope undermines generalization claims: restricted to 2-player games, only Qwen-4B model, 200 optimization steps, and simplified game variants

Transfer learning mechanism poorly understood: the connection between strategic games and mathematical reasoning is intuitive but not rigorously established; only anecdotal qualitative evidence provided
Inconsistent and limited baseline comparisons: primary baseline (SPIRAL) sometimes outperforms MARS; missing comparisons with other multi-agent RL and curriculum learning approaches
Reward design obscures the actual learning signal: auxiliary rewards (format regularization, length penalties) could substantially confound results; no ablation on reward components
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear if reported differences are statistically meaningful
Generalization claims exceed evidence: title and abstract claim broad 'generalizable' capabilities but evaluation limited to 2 specific multi-agent frameworks
Missing critical analyses: no sample efficiency study, computational cost comparison, investigation of which games contribute most, or analysis of failure modes
Ablation studies show inconsistent patterns (sometimes removing components helps, sometimes hurts) without clear explanations; fixed-opponent ablation could be more thorough

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in multi-turn, multi-agent RL (credit assignment and advantage variance)
Comprehensive experimental scope with diverse games (adversarial and cooperative), held-out generalization tests, and integration with multiple downstream multi-agent systems
Balanced curriculum including both competitive and cooperative games, offering broader training signal than prior work (SPIRAL)
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and game prompts; code promised for reproducibility
Demonstrates consistent positive results across games (28.7% improvement on held-out games) and downstream reasoning benchmarks (10% AIME, 12.5% GPQA)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contributions (sum-then-normalize advantage estimation and per-role normalization) are straightforward modifications to GRPO lacking methodological depth
Weak baseline comparisons: only SPIRAL as primary baseline; missing comparisons with other multi-agent RL methods, game-theoretic approaches, and related self-play work like SPAG
Inconsistent downstream results: SPIRAL achieves 51.20 on single-agent AIME vs. some MARS variants at 46.50-48.40; generalist model doesn't consistently outperform specialists
Limited scope: only 2-player games with constrained action spaces; unclear how findings scale to complex N-player environments (acknowledged but unaddressed limitation)
No statistical rigor: missing error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests; some ablation effects appear within noise margins (e.g., 75.30→74.60 ≈0.9%)
Unclear transfer mechanism: paper lacks mechanistic understanding of why/when game-playing improves reasoning; Table 2 examples appear anecdotal rather than systematic

Overstated generalization claims: improvements are modest (1-12%) and the connection between game-playing and reasoning is not rigorously established; held-out games are just harder versions of training games, not true out-of-domain generalization

Incomplete evaluation: single-model evaluation (Qwen-4B only); limited multi-agent system coverage (only MAD and AutoGen); reward design complexity unexplored (format penalties, length penalties); sensitivity to hyperparameters unknown
Superficial pattern analysis: Table 2 examples lack systematic measurement of behavior consistency; no analysis of failure cases or when learned patterns don't transfer
Missing critical analysis: computational cost vs. single-agent RL not discussed; no justification for reward component weights; limited exploration of design choices

strengths: Well-motivated technical contributions addressing legitimate challenges in multi-agent RL for LLMs (credit assignment and advantage variance)
Principled turn-level advantage estimator design with theoretical grounding in GAE equivalence and zero-mean advantages
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning game performance, out-of-distribution generalization, integration with real multi-agent systems, and reasoning benchmarks
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements across games (28.7% on Leduc Hold'em) and reasoning tasks (10% AIME, 12.5% GPQA-Diamond)
Excellent reproducibility commitment with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and promised code/model release
Insightful qualitative analysis demonstrating skill transfer through emergent patterns (role-awareness, intent recognition)
Solid ablation studies validating both key algorithmic components independently
Natural extension of prior work (SPIRAL) to both cooperative and competitive settings with unified framework
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: turn-level advantage estimator is a straightforward reordering of normalization steps; agent-specific normalization is an engineering best practice rather than fundamental innovation
Severely constrained scope: only 2-player games with small, discrete action spaces; scalability to N-player or large action spaces entirely unexplored
Modest baseline comparisons: only SPIRAL compared; improvements often <2% on reasoning benchmarks; no comparison with alternative approaches like prompt engineering
Single base model (Qwen-4B): generalization to different model families and sizes unclear
Unclear mechanistic explanation for game-to-reasoning generalization: why should Tic-Tac-Toe improve AIME performance?
Contradicts stated goal of minimizing reward engineering: multiple components with manually tuned hyperparameters (lmin=11, lmax=2048, α=0.5) lack justification; no sensitivity analysis
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds reported; significance of improvements not established
Incomplete analysis of design choices: why is generalist model superior? Which games contribute to which reasoning skills?
Scalability concerns: training on 8 H100s; unclear how approach scales to larger models or more complex environments
Incremental relative to SPIRAL: main contribution is adding cooperative games plus two engineering fixes rather than novel algorithmic insight

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning strategic ability, generalization to multi-agent systems, reasoning pattern analysis, and thorough ablations
Clear problem formulation addressing genuine challenges in multi-turn, multi-agent RL (credit assignment and agent-specific advantage estimation)
Well-designed game portfolio including both cooperative and competitive games, providing evidence that both are necessary for effective transfer
Simple yet effective algorithmic contributions: turn-level 'sum-then-normalize' advantage estimator theoretically grounded in GAE, and agent-specific normalization for heterogeneous roles
Strong reproducibility efforts with promised code/model release, detailed hyperparameters across appendices, and implementation details
Scaling validation to 8B models demonstrating generalizability beyond 4B experiments
Meaningful qualitative analysis of skill transfer (role understanding, intent recognition) with concrete examples from games to downstream tasks
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: individual components represent straightforward modifications to GRPO; agent-specific normalization is similar to concurrent SPIRAL's RAE; Appendix E shows algorithm alone insufficient without appropriate game selection

Modest performance improvements: single-agent gains of 1-3%, multi-agent average of 3.5%; headline figures (10% AIME, 6.6% GPQA) appear cherry-picked; Table 1 shows SPIRAL competitive on many benchmarks; some metrics degrade (AMC: 36.70→33.30)
Narrow experimental scope: only 2-player games tested; claim of 'generalizable multi-agent reasoning' questionable given training restriction; authors acknowledge but dismiss this limitation

Unclear generalization mechanism: lack of deep explanation for why strategic reasoning in games transfers to mathematical problem-solving; cross-category transfer only anecdotally demonstrated; connection between game-theoretic skills and reasoning benchmarks underexplored

Reward engineering undermines 'unsupervised learning' claims: large negative penalty (-10.0) for invalid format, parameterized length penalty with apparent arbitrary choices (lmin=11, lmax=2048, α=0.5); Appendix G shows sensitivity to these hyperparameters
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; seed strategy unclear; small test sets on some benchmarks (AIME ~40 examples) could obscure noise vs. true improvements
Weak baseline representation: SPIRAL is concurrent work; no comparison with other RL approaches for LLMs; Qwen3-4B baseline relatively weak; marginal improvements over MT-GRPO in Appendix F

Limited mechanistic understanding: Table 2 provides only two qualitative examples of skill transfer; insufficient analysis of what game properties or reasoning patterns specifically predict downstream improvements

strengths: Addresses well-motivated problem: multi-turn, multi-agent RL for LLMs is genuinely understudied and challenging
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 games, 2 MAS frameworks, multiple benchmarks, extensive ablations, and scaling to 8B model
Strong cross-categorical generalization evidence: Tic-Tac-Toe specialist transfers to Mini Hanabi, suggesting genuine skill learning
Insightful qualitative analysis: Table 2 demonstrates emergence of interpretable skills (role understanding, intent recognition)
Good failure mode analysis: Figure 5 quantifies improvements in inter-agent misalignment, providing mechanistic insights
Thorough reproducibility: Promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, implementation via established ROLL framework
Systematic ablations: Validates design choices through self-play vs. fixed-opponent and component removal studies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Turn-level advantage estimator is standard GAE with γ=1, λ=1 (acknowledged by authors). Agent-specific normalization is straightforward per-role separation, similar to concurrent SPIRAL's RAE. The sum-then-normalize improvement is incremental.

Modest downstream improvements: 3.5% average across benchmarks; largest gains (10% AIME) inconsistent across settings. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests—robustness across seeds unknown

Weak mechanistic understanding of transfer: Paper demonstrates transfer occurs but provides limited insight into why game training helps reasoning. Role understanding/intent recognition feel like post-hoc rationalizations rather than principled explanations. Why Tic-Tac-Toe skills help AIME remains unclear.

Reward engineering contradicts claims: Despite claiming 'unsupervised game outcomes,' includes tuned action format regularization (-10.0 penalty) and response length penalty (α=0.5 sensitivity shown in Appendix G: Mini Hanabi 50.48%→38.18%). This undermines the minimal reward engineering narrative.

Limited scope of investigation: Only Qwen-4B in main results; two-player games only (n-player generalization unexamined); evaluation restricted to math/QA benchmarks (no code, dialogue, open-ended reasoning); game selection appears arbitrary with no systematic ablation

Unclear contribution separation: Success origin unclear—is it algorithmic improvements, game selection, or training setup? Appendix E decoupling shows RAE+games performs similarly (54.33% Mini Hanabi), suggesting algorithm may matter less than claimed.

Overclaimed generalization: Tested only within MAD/AutoGen frameworks; not general multi-agent capability. Claims of 'groundbreaking impact' and '10% improvement' in abstract oversell 3.5% average gain.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: SPIRAL is concurrent work; no comparison with other multi-agent RL methods or alternative LLM reasoning improvement approaches. Fixed-opponent severe degradation (Table 3) unexplored.
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Cannot assess whether improvements are robust or potentially noise.
Presentation issues: Dense paper with scattered results; Table 1 difficult to parse; connection between strategic games and reasoning could be clearer; some overclaimed language

strengths: Comprehensive and thorough experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions (games, benchmarks, frameworks, scales, ablations)
Clear problem formulation with well-articulated technical challenges (long-horizon credit assignment and agent-specific advantage estimation)
Simple yet effective technical contributions validated through comparisons with concurrent work (MT-GRPO, SPIRAL)
Strong mechanistic insight provided through failure mode analysis and qualitative reasoning pattern examination
Consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks and both cooperative/competitive frameworks
Excellent reproducibility with promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, and complete implementation details
Effective scaling validation to larger models (8B) demonstrating robustness of approach
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - primarily engineering improvements on GRPO rather than fundamental algorithmic advances; sum-then-normalize is similar to existing process supervision approaches
Restrictive scope limited to 2-player games despite real multi-agent systems often involving 3+ agents; unclear whether learned skills adequately prepare for more complex coordination
Modest downstream improvements in many cases (1-3.5% averages with some outliers at 10%), making it unclear if gains reflect genuine reasoning enhancement versus coincidental benchmark alignment

Insufficient mechanistic analysis of transfer - limited exploration of which game characteristics enable transfer, why specific games chosen, or which game features map to which reasoning improvements
Missing statistical rigor - no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported; variance across random seeds and statistical significance of improvements unclear
Computational cost and training efficiency not discussed; practical comparison with alternatives not provided
Game selection and reward engineering involve multiple hand-crafted components whose individual impact not fully characterized; reward normalization choices not fully justified
Limited scope of failure mode analysis restricted to single benchmark (GPQA-Diamond) in single framework (MAD)
